t: It's three in the morning, and you're slicing a bagel in the hospital break room. The knife slips.
graphic: night break room, 3D bagel and knife, the slip

t: Half an inch of your finger is just... gone.
graphic: hero stares at his hand (cartoon: bandage-white stump, no blood), nurse freezes

t: You're a doctor. You know exactly what to do. Ice, gauze, call the surgeon. But before you can move, your finger starts to itch.
graphic: he grabs gauze, stops, looks at the finger

t: Then it grows. Bone, then skin, then a tiny new nail. Forty seconds. Not even a scar.
graphic: close-up: fingertip grows back in 3 stages, sparkle

t: The night nurse drops her coffee. You drop the bagel.
graphic: two drops, coffee splash on the floor, bagel rolls and stays

t: So what if you could regrow any part of your body?
graphic: title words, hero in a spotlight looking at his hand

t: Sounds impossible? Not for everyone. An axolotl, a smiling little salamander from Mexico, can regrow a leg, part of its heart, even pieces of its brain. Without a single scar.
graphic: aquarium: 3D axolotl, its leg grows back; labels LEG / HEART / BRAIN

t: In eighteen ninety-eight, scientist Thomas Hunt Morgan cut a flatworm into tiny pieces. A piece just one two-hundred-seventy-ninth of the worm grew into a whole new worm.
graphic: sepia lab 1898, Morgan at a microscope, worm sliced, "1/279" pops, piece becomes a worm

t: Today, that's you. Only you're a doctor.
graphic: Doctor ROO in a white coat, "THAT'S YOU" / "DOCTOR" tags, counter appears: REGROWN 1

t: First, you need to know how it works. So you do what any scientist would do. You experiment on yourself.
graphic: small lab, ROO rolls up a sleeve, notebook

t: Your colleague, Dr. Reyes, takes a tiny slice of skin from your arm, then stitches the wound shut, nice and neat.
graphic: Reyes (not yellow, not ginger) with tweezers, needle and thread

t: Nothing happens. A week later, you just have a scar.
graphic: calendar page flips 7 days, scar line on the arm

t: So she takes another slice, and this time leaves the wound open under a bandage. Twenty seconds later, the skin is back.
graphic: bandage, timer 0:20, bandage off: clean skin

t: Rule number one: a stitched wound scars. An open one regrows.
graphic: rule card: needle = scar, bandage = regrow

t: Weirdly, real doctors noticed something similar. In nineteen seventy-four, Dr. Cynthia Illingworth in Sheffield reported that children's cut-off fingertips often grew back, if surgeons just left them alone instead of stitching them closed.
graphic: 1974 card, children's hospital, child's finger in a dressing

t: It works in kids up to about eleven years old. Nail, fingerprint and all.
graphic: age bar 0–11, fingertip with a fingerprint

t: Rule number two shows up at lunch. You're starving. You eat two burgers, a pizza, and half the vending machine.
graphic: cafeteria: he eats with his hands, stack of empty plates

t: A new body part has to be built from something, and that something is whatever you eat. Every regrowth costs you a mountain of food.
graphic: infographic: plate → arrow → finger

t: Rule number three shows up at a softball game. A ball knocks out your front tooth. By dinner, a new one has pushed in.
graphic: park, ball hits, tooth flies and lands on the grass, dinner table, new tooth

t: Not a copy of the old tooth. A brand-new one. No filling, no stains. Whatever regrows comes back factory new.
graphic: old tooth (filling, stain) vs new tooth, "FACTORY NEW" stamp inside the card

t: Real scientists are chasing this exact trick. In twenty twenty-four, doctors in Kyoto began the first human trial of a drug meant to help people grow new teeth. They hope it could reach patients around twenty thirty.
graphic: Kyoto clinic card, 2024 → 2030 timeline

t: Now, a doctor who can regrow anything starts asking a dangerous question. What else could I give away?
graphic: ROO at an X-ray light box, looking at his own body

t: Here's a real fact: the human liver regrows. A living donor can give part of theirs to a patient, and in about two months it grows back to almost full size.
graphic: liver diagram: part removed, grows back, "~2 MONTHS"

t: Yours grows back overnight.
graphic: same diagram, timer "1 NIGHT"

t: So you become a donor. A slice of liver in March. Another in April. By December, you've given away more than one whole liver, and you're still using yours.
graphic: wall calendar months flip, liver icons pile up

t: Then you try a kidney. A normal kidney can't regrow at all. Yours is back in four days.
graphic: kidney card, days 1–4 ticking

t: The waiting list at your hospital gets shorter every week. The newspapers call you "the Spare Parts Doctor."
graphic: waiting-list board losing names; newspaper held in hands

t: And companies come calling. A man in a very expensive suit offers you a billion dollars for a vial of your cells.
graphic: office, 3D vial, check with many zeros

t: Real labs are already trying to grow body parts. In two thousand six, Dr. Anthony Atala reported seven young patients living with bladders grown from their own cells.
graphic: lab: cells → scaffold → bladder, "7 PATIENTS, 2006"

t: And in twenty twenty-two, a young woman in Texas received an ear that was 3D-printed from her own cartilage cells.
graphic: 3D printer printing an ear, 2022 tag

t: But real labs are slow, and you're not. You turn down the man in the suit. You've got patients waiting.
graphic: he slides the check back, walks out to the ward

t: Then, one Tuesday, Dr. Reyes looks at your blood test and goes quiet.
graphic: Reyes at a screen, her face drops

t: Your cells are dividing faster than anything she's ever seen. Faster than a deer antler.
graphic: microscope view of fast-dividing cells

t: Antlers are one of the fastest-growing tissues of any mammal. Up to two centimeters a day.
graphic: forest, deer, antler growing with a ruler "2 CM/DAY"

t: And in twenty nineteen, scientists found that antlers grow using genes that look a lot like the genes of bone cancer. The deer just know how to keep them in check.
graphic: gene strip: ANTLER vs BONE CANCER, matching bars

t: Fast growth and cancer are two sides of the same coin. In nineteen eighty-six, a doctor named Harold Dvorak described tumors as "wounds that do not heal."
graphic: quote card, sepia note

t: "Every time you regrow something," Reyes says, "you roll the dice."
graphic: 3D dice roll on the desk and stay there

t: You start counting. Forty-one regrowths. Forty-one rolls of the dice.
graphic: counter above his head ticks to 41

t: Three weeks later, you find it. A small, hard lump on your forearm, right where that second slice of skin grew back.
graphic: bathroom mirror, morning, he feels his arm

t: Your hands shake while Reyes cuts it out. It isn't cancer. Not yet. It's just skin that didn't know when to stop.
graphic: procedure room, lab report "BENIGN"

t: This time, she stitches the wound shut. On purpose. A scar is a stop sign.
graphic: needle and thread, "STOP" sign-shaped scar card

t: Maybe that's why we scar at all. One theory says mammals traded regrowing for something faster and safer: a quick patch that stops infection, and keeps runaway growth in check.
graphic: axolotl vs human card, "THEORY" label

t: So you decide to stop. No more regrowing. Ever.
graphic: he puts the counter away in a drawer

t: And that's exactly when Lily arrives. She's seven. Her liver is failing, and there's no donor for her on the list.
graphic: ER doors, a little girl on a raised bed, half-sitting, eyes open

t: Except you. Same blood type. A perfect match.
graphic: match card: two blood bags, check mark

t: A normal donor would grow that piece back over a couple of months. You'll grow it back in one night. Another roll of the dice.
graphic: dice on the table again

t: Reyes sits down next to you in the empty cafeteria. "You don't owe anyone this," she says.
graphic: night cafeteria, two people sitting properly on chairs

t: You look at the bagel on your tray. The same kind that started all of this.
graphic: 3D bagel on the tray, close-up

t: Then you sign the form.
graphic: pen in hand, signature

t: The surgery takes nine hours. By morning, Lily's new liver is working. And yours has already grown back.
graphic: OR, clock 9 hours, monitor beats; dawn

t: For a week, you check your skin every morning. No lumps. The counter stops at forty-two. And that's where you leave it.
graphic: mirror, counter 42, he turns off the light

t: Here's the twist, though. You don't need a superpower to regrow body parts. You already can. A little.
graphic: ROO faces camera, the counter fades

t: Your liver regrows. Your skin keeps replacing itself. A broken bone rebuilds itself, and a rib can even grow back, if surgeons leave its outer lining in place.
graphic: x-ray infographic lighting up liver, skin, bone, rib

t: Cut nerves regrow too, about a millimeter a day. And kids' fingertips grow back, if we just leave them alone.
graphic: nerve line growing, "1 MM/DAY"

t: The power isn't missing. It's switched off. And scientists are looking for the switch.
graphic: big switch in the OFF position

t: In twenty twenty-two, a team led by Michael Levin at Tufts University put a tiny dome filled with five drugs over a frog's cut leg, for just twenty-four hours. Over the next eighteen months, the frog regrew a working leg.
graphic: lab: frog, dome, 24 h, months flip, leg regrows

t: It wasn't perfect. But a frog that shouldn't regrow a leg did. And mammals are next on the list.
graphic: frog swims with the new leg

t: A year later, Lily is back in your ER. She caught her finger in a car door. The tip is gone.
graphic: ER, Lily (same look), bandaged finger

t: The surgeon on duty reaches for the needle and thread. You stop him. "Leave it open. Just a dressing."
graphic: hand stops the needle

t: Eight weeks later, Lily shows you a brand-new fingertip. Nail and all. No superpower needed.
graphic: Lily waves the finger, ROO smiles

t: So if you could regrow one body part, which one would you pick? Tell me in the comments.
graphic: question card with ROO

t: And subscribe.
graphic: subscribe button (3D)
